title: North Sikkim permits explained for Indians and foreigners
meta_description: Who needs which permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen, Gurudongmar and Dzongu, what documents to send, how long it takes, and the rules foreigners must follow.
summary: Indian citizens need a Protected Area Permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu and Gurudongmar, filed only through a registered Sikkim operator a day or more ahead. Foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit plus the North Sikkim permit, travel in groups of two or more and cannot visit Gurudongmar. Dzongu needs its own permit.

sections.heading: Why North Sikkim needs permits
paras: North Sikkim, now officially Mangan district, shares a long border with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, and much of the land above the tree line is an Indian Army zone. For that reason the government restricts who can travel beyond a line of checkposts north of Mangan and how. Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu and Gurudongmar Lake all lie in this protected area. The lower stretch of the North Sikkim Highway, with Kabi Lungchok, Phodong, Mangan and Singhik, is open to Indians without a special permit.

The permits are not difficult, but they shape how you plan. You cannot walk up to a counter and get one on the day, you cannot travel independently, and the rules for foreigners are stricter than for Indians. Everything below is the rule as we understand it in October 2026. Permit systems in Sikkim change with security, weather and road conditions, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Indian citizens: how the permit works
paras: Indian citizens apply for the North Sikkim Protected Area Permit only through a registered Sikkim tour operator. You cannot apply yourself. The operator collects a copy of a government photo ID for each traveller, such as an Aadhaar card, passport, voter ID or driving licence, plus two passport-size photographs, and files the application with the authorities in Gangtok. Children need ID too; a school ID or birth certificate is usually accepted.

Allow at least one full day. Most operators ask for documents a few days ahead by WhatsApp or email and collect the permit on the morning you leave Gangtok, which is why North Sikkim departures usually leave at 10–11 am. Same-day permits are not issued. Permit processing costs roughly ₹200–300 per person through the operator, indicative 2026, and is normally built into the package price.

Carry the original ID you submitted. Police and army checkposts on the way, including those near Mangan, Chungthang, Lachen and Thangu, can match your face to the permit. Your driver holds the permit itself and shows it at each stop.

sections.heading: Foreign nationals: the extra steps
paras: Every foreign national entering Sikkim needs a Restricted Area Permit. It is issued at the Rangpo checkpost on the main road from Siliguri, through the state's online system, and through some Indian missions abroad, with your passport and Indian visa. It is valid for a limited period, which can be extended in Gangtok. Keep several photocopies of your passport and visa.

For North Sikkim you then need a further permit, filed by an approved Sikkim operator, and you must usually travel in a group of at least two. That group can be your own party of two in a private car. Foreign nationals can usually visit Lachung and Yumthang and go up the Lachen valley as far as Thangu. Gurudongmar Lake is not open to foreign nationals, and mixed groups follow the foreign rule, so the whole car turns at Thangu or splits for the day. Zero Point rules for foreigners have changed several times. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The Dzongu permit
paras: Dzongu, the Lepcha reserve across the Teesta from Mangan, has its own entry permit, separate from the Lachung and Lachen permit. Every visitor who is not a Lepcha from Dzongu needs it. In practice your homestay arranges it with the district authorities from scanned ID and photographs. Send them at least a week before you arrive, because there is no permit counter at the Dzongu check-post. A nominal fee may apply.

Foreign nationals have been able to visit Dzongu in some years and not others, sometimes only in groups through an operator. If you are not Indian, ask the homestay to confirm the current position in writing before you book anything else.

sections.heading: On the road: checkposts and time limits
paras: Under the order in force in September 2026, vehicles must cross the Toong checkpost, between Mangan and Chungthang, by 4 pm in both directions. That is why Gangtok departures leave by late morning and why return days start early. Night driving beyond the checkposts is not allowed. If you arrive late, you may have to sleep in Mangan or Singhik.

At each checkpost your driver shows the permit and the police or army may count heads or check IDs. Follow instructions, do not photograph army posts or bridges, and keep your ID within reach. Above Thangu and on the Yumthang road, soldiers may also tell you where you can stand and for how long.

sections.heading: When permits are suspended
paras: Permits are not issued when the roads are unsafe. Since the October 2023 South Lhonak flood, that has happened often. Lachen stayed closed to tourists for most of the next three years and reopened in 2026. Landslides in 2024 and 2025 closed Lachung for months. In 2025 permits for Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point resumed on 8 September, and in 2026 permits for Lachen resumed around 10–11 September.

Monsoon, from June to August, is the usual time for suspensions, but heavy snow can stop permits in winter too, especially for Lachen and Gurudongmar. A suspension can be announced the evening before you travel. Book refundable flights and hotels, keep a spare day in Gangtok and check current status before you travel.
list: Send ID copies and two photographs per person to your operator at least three days ahead.
Foreign nationals: get the Restricted Area Permit at Rangpo or online before anything else.
Book Dzongu permits through your homestay a week ahead.
Carry original ID and several photocopies on the trip.
Plan to leave Gangtok by late morning and to cross Toong by 4 pm.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for North Sikkim
faqs.a: Yes, for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu and Gurudongmar. Indian citizens need a Protected Area Permit, applied for only through a registered Sikkim tour operator with a photo ID copy and two photographs each. No permit is needed for Kabi Lungchok, Phodong, Mangan or Singhik. Dzongu needs its own permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does a North Sikkim permit take
faqs.a: Usually one to two days. Operators collect your documents a few days ahead and pick up the permit on the morning you leave Gangtok, which is why trips depart at about 10–11 am. Same-day permits are not issued. In peak weeks or after a reopening, allow extra time. Send documents early by WhatsApp or email to avoid losing a day.

faqs.q: Can I get a North Sikkim permit myself
faqs.a: No. Indian citizens and foreign nationals alike must apply through a registered Sikkim tour operator, who files the application and arranges the registered vehicle and driver you must travel with. Hotels in Gangtok usually work with operators and can arrange it. You can still choose between a shared group package and a private car.

No. Gurudongmar Lake is not open to foreign nationals, as generally understood and as operators apply the rule today. Foreign nationals with the required permits can usually go up the Lachen valley as far as Thangu, at about 3,900 m. In a mixed group of Indians and foreigners, the car either turns at Thangu or the group splits. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do foreigners get the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit
faqs.a: At the Rangpo checkpost on the main road from Siliguri, through Sikkim's online permit system, or through some Indian missions abroad with your visa. You need your passport, Indian visa and photographs. It is valid for a limited period and can be extended in Gangtok. North Sikkim then needs a further permit through an approved operator. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What documents do I need for the North Sikkim permit
faqs.a: Indian citizens need a copy of a government photo ID, such as an Aadhaar card, passport, voter ID or driving licence, and two passport-size photographs per person. Children need ID too; a school ID or birth certificate is usually accepted. Foreign nationals need passport and visa copies, photographs and the Restricted Area Permit. Carry originals on the trip.

faqs.q: Is Zero Point included in the Lachung permit
faqs.a: For Indian citizens, Zero Point is normally covered by the Lachung and Yumthang permit, but you pay a separate vehicle charge locally, about ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle, indicative 2026. Access is decided season by season and is often closed after snow and from about mid-December. For foreign nationals the rules have varied. Ask your operator on the morning.

faqs.q: What is the 4 pm rule at Toong checkpost
faqs.a: Under the order in force in September 2026, vehicles must cross the Toong checkpost, between Mangan and Chungthang, by 4 pm in both directions. If you are late, you cannot continue and may need to sleep in Mangan or Singhik. That is why trips leave Gangtok by late morning and return days start early. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are North Sikkim permits issued in the monsoon
faqs.a: Often not. Permits for Lachung and Lachen are frequently suspended in June, July and August because of landslides, sometimes for weeks. In 2025 Lachung permits resumed on 8 September, and in 2026 Lachen permits resumed around 10–11 September. Suspensions can come at short notice in any season. Check current status before you travel.
